## The idea

Play A minor on the white keys and the scale reaches A without a semitone below
the final note. The arrival is softer than B to C in the previous lesson.
Composers often alter the scale when they want that stronger pull. The result is
a family of minor scales rather than one immutable list.

*Natural minor* uses the major-scale step pattern rotated to begin on its sixth
degree. *Harmonic minor* raises degree 7 on the way up and down. *Melodic minor*
raises degrees 6 and 7 while ascending, then uses natural minor while descending.
Those labels sounded like historical clutter to me until I diffed the arrays.
One changed element supplies harmonic minor's leading tone; two changed elements
smooth the melodic climb.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 108
use_synth :piano

define :play_phrase do |notes|
  notes.each do |pitch|
    play pitch, release: 0.35
    sleep 0.5
  end
end

natural = [57, 59, 60, 62, 64, 65, 67, 69]
harmonic = [57, 59, 60, 62, 64, 65, 68, 69]
melodic_up = [57, 59, 60, 62, 64, 66, 68, 69]
melodic_down = natural.reverse

puts "harmonic changes: #{natural.zip(harmonic).select { |a, b| a != b }}"
puts "melodic changes: #{natural.zip(melodic_up).select { |a, b| a != b }}"

[natural, harmonic, melodic_up].each do |notes|
  play_phrase notes
  play_phrase notes.reverse
  sleep 1
end

play_phrase melodic_up + melodic_down.drop(1)

tune_degrees = [0, 2, 4, 3, 2, 5, 6, 7, 4, 3, 2, 1, 6, 7, 0]
[natural, harmonic, melodic_up].each do |scale_notes|
  play_phrase tune_degrees.map { |degree| scale_notes[degree] }
  sleep 1
end
```

Natural minor gives the tune an even, modal shape. Harmonic minor makes the last
step to A more insistent and creates a wide three-semitone gap between F and
G-sharp. Melodic minor fills that gap with F-sharp on the ascent. The printed
diff shows how little data changes between the three versions.

## Change one thing

1. Lower harmonic minor's G-sharp back to G in the final two notes only. The
   tune still uses harmonic minor elsewhere, but its closing gesture loses the
   leading-tone pull.
2. Use `:prophet` instead of `:piano` and set `release: 0.8`. Sustained notes make
   the augmented second between F and G-sharp overlap. Listen for the interval's
   colour rather than treating it as an array difference.
3. Transpose every array by adding 5. The scale family moves from A to D while
   all internal differences remain fixed.

## Why it works

Natural minor begins from degree 6 of its relative major. Rotating the major
formula produces `2, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 2`. Its seventh degree lies two semitones
below the tonic. Raising that degree changes the last interval to one semitone,
recreating the leading tone heard in major.

That repair produces a new melodic issue: degree 6 to raised degree 7 spans
three semitones. Harmonic writing can use the striking gap, while a rising melody
often prefers smaller motion. Melodic minor raises degree 6 as well, producing
whole-tone steps through 5, 6, and 7. On the descent, the leading tone has no
upward destination, so the natural form returns.

The code keeps each form as explicit data. That is clearer than burying the
alterations inside a renderer. `zip` aligns positions, and `select` exposes the
changed entries. The tune then consumes any compatible eight-note array, which
separates melodic shape from scale choice.

## Take it further

Write `minor_forms(root)` that returns a hash with `:natural`, `:harmonic`,
`:melodic_up`, and `:melodic_down`. Generate the values from step formulas rather
than copying arrays. Verify that the natural and harmonic forms differ at one
index and that natural and melodic-up differ at two. Play a two-octave ascent
and descent in E minor using the correct melodic direction.
